title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit that implemented conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap, provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy to test whether contamination controls change validator‑measured success on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The executed run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one model generation reused across baseline/guarded episodes), which materially collapsed independent generation variance. Consequently, no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and no guarded exclusions or replacements were performed. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed a deterministic validator (baseline = 150/150; guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We explicitly record and explain the preregistration→execution deviation (planned public‑item sampling → executed synthetic sampling; planned independent per‑condition generation → executed shared generation), reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as degenerate/untestable under the executed semantics, document detector persistence behavior (per‑item fuzzy overlap scores were persisted only on threshold crossings), and give artifact‑anchored recommendations (provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, persist per‑item scores, multi‑model replication, paraphrase‑robust detectors) to make future contamination audits informative for web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration synthesis, configuration repair). Reliable operational claims depend on evaluations that are free from dataset contamination (items or templated prompts present in model training data) and from construct invalidity (benchmarks dominated by templated, low‑complexity items). Recent surveys call for contamination‑aware, verifier‑backed evaluations and preregistered audit procedures.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered a confirmatory study (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to answer: under conservative deterministic detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, (1) how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and (2) how much does applying those controls change a hosted LLM's validator pass rate? We report an artifact‑verified execution, an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that documents a procedural deviation that rendered the primary confirmatory test degenerate, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to increase audit sensitivity in future runs.

Bounded claims. The executed sample used synthetic, provenance‑stable tasks and shared generation semantics; the observed null result therefore applies only to this execution regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑driven NetOps and verification. Prior system and benchmark work shows LLMs can produce device configurations and propose repairs; combining LLMs with formal or deterministic validators (Header Space Analysis family, localized subspecification) or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair safety vs naive generation. Surveys and benchmark proposals emphasize contamination and construct‑validity risks for LLM evaluations and recommend deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, and provenance tracing.

Positioning. Unlike broad capability benchmarks that compare models, this paper is a tightly preregistered audit of contamination controls implemented end‑to‑end and archived with deterministic validators and reconciliation artifacts. Its primary scientific contribution is an artifact‑anchored diagnosis of why a preregistered confirmatory test became uninformative under the executed semantics and what concrete, implementable design changes are required to make future confirmations sensitive to web‑sourced contamination.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study preregistered a paired binary design: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, analysis executor = paired_binary_analysis_v1, primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided, companion paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned confirmatory accounting: task_count = 150 items, planned_episode_count = 300 (baseline + guarded), maximum_model_calls = 300 (two independent generations per item when executed).

Sampling, generator, and execution semantics (preregistered vs executed). The preregistration allowed deterministic synthetic generation but listed four public OpenAlex benchmark records in benchmark_scope for sampling. The executed run, however, sampled items produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each sampled task carries a provenance marker source_identifier with a "synthetic-netops:" prefix (recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Critically, the executed model_configuration.json sets independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), so the pipeline performed a single shared generation per item and reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes when no high‑confidence contamination flags triggered exclusions or replacements. The joint effect of synthetic provenance and shared generation is documented in execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts (see artifact paths below). These execution facts (sampling provenance and shared generation) are the principal preregistration→execution deviations we record and analyze.

Contamination detectors and guarded policy. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality (canonicalize whitespace/tokens; exact match = high confidence), (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (lower thresholds 0.65, 0.50 for sensitivity), and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics against public archive timestamps. The guarded policy excluded only high‑confidence flags (exact OR 5‑gram ≥ 0.80) and deterministically replaced excluded items using deterministic retemplating + topology augmentation (replacement acceptance required embedding cosine ≥ 0.85). The implemented detector persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs and replacement traces only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred (detector persistence behavior is recorded in the transformation manifest). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred in this run, the per‑item overlap table was not materialized in the archive (see Results and artifact pointers).

Deterministic validator and scoring. The verification oracle deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs parse→state update simulation and checks the task's required_final_state and workflow constraints (sequence, protected interfaces, group constraints). The scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation requires both final‑state agreement on allowed fields and respect of transient/workflow constraints; the validator produces a binary pass/fail and detailed traces per episode (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration). All validator traces and raw responses were archived and are the basis of the binary outcomes used in analysis.

Analysis plan and missingness. Primary analysis used McNemar on paired counts (n11,n10,n01,n00) and paired bootstrap CI as described above. The preregistered missingness policy included one automated retry for transient provider failures; execution logs show zero failed episodes. Planned sensitivity analyses (fuzzy threshold sweep; failure-as‑zero) remained feasible but are uninformative in this execution because no discordant pairs were observed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the pipeline used model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two independent generations per item; provider call accounting and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm these counts (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json).

Contamination detector outcomes and persistence behavior. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows. The implemented detector persisted per‑item fuzzy overlap scores and detailed overlap tables only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred; that persistence policy is recorded in the transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json). Because no threshold crossings were recorded, a global per‑item overlap table is absent from the archive for this run—this is an explicit artifact of the detector implementation and not a data loss. The archive does contain the detector control artifacts and the contamination_summary.csv (empty) that document this behavior.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics (degeneracy). deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Primary estimand (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We explicitly reclassify this primary confirmatory test as degenerate/untestable for detecting generation‑level contamination under the executed semantics because shared_initial_candidate generation mechanically produces identical baseline/guarded outputs absent exclusion‑triggered replacements.

Representative episode diagnostics. Representative archived episodes (e.g., pair‑000001 task‑000001 in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/scoring/*) show identical normalized_response and normalized_reference_answer and full validator_trace fields confirming parse counts and final state—these artifacts substantiate the reported binary pass counts and validator behavior.

Absence of per‑item overlap distribution. Because the detector persisted detailed per‑item overlap outputs only when thresholds were crossed, the archive does not contain a full per‑item overlap distribution for this run. The absence is explained by the recorded detector persistence policy (execution/transformation_manifest.json) and the empty analysis/contamination_summary.csv; thus we report the documented absence rather than invent overlap statistics.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory test was uninformative. Two executed facts archived in the bundle jointly explain the observed concordance: (1) the confirmatory sample is provenance‑stable synthetic (each task manifests source_identifier with prefix "synthetic-netops:"); and (2) the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), resulting in one model generation per item reused for both baseline and guarded episodes when no high‑confidence flags triggered replacements. Both facts are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json and create a mechanical collapse of baseline vs guarded discordance, making the primary paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Detector persistence tradeoffs and recommended changes. The implemented detector persisted detailed overlap outputs only on threshold crossings to limit stored artifact size; this choice is recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json. While practical for many runs, it prevents post‑hoc inspection of how near items were to the high‑confidence threshold when no flags occurred. To increase interpretability and audit sensitivity we recommend: (a) persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores for every sampled item regardless of threshold crossings; (b) sample provenance‑rich public items (URL/DOI/timestamp present) to enable meaningful provenance heuristics; (c) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded outputs are independently realized (increase model_calls_used accordingly); (d) expand to multiple model instances and random seeds to raise expected discordance and power; and (e) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from the archived execution facts (model_calls_used = 150; empty contamination_summary.csv; lack of per‑item overlap table) and is implementable within the same framework.

Statistical interpretation and power implications. The preregistration included power guidance showing that independent per‑condition generation and multi‑model replication materially improve detectability of modest paired differences (~4–6 percentage points under conservative assumptions). Under shared generation semantics, the probability of observing discordant pairs falls even when contamination exists in a stochastic or paraphrase‑sensitive form; the recorded CI [0.0,0.0] and p = 1.0 therefore reflect a degenerate sample rather than evidence that contamination is absent in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Operational caution. Passing the deterministic validator confirms the configurations satisfy the checked constraints for these synthetic tasks, but neither this run nor the validator trace implies production readiness or absence of other semantic regressions outside the validator's scope. Auditors aiming to evaluate contamination prevalence in public benchmarks must combine provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, cross‑model checks, and human adjudication to obtain generalizable evidence.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluations. The run observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline and guarded). This null result is artifact‑grounded and stems from a preregistration→execution deviation (executed synthetic sampling and shared_initial_candidate generation) that made the prespecified primary test degenerate/untestable for detecting generation‑level contamination. We explicitly document the deviation, the detector persistence behavior, and the reconciliation artifacts; and we prescribe concrete, implementable changes—provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, persisting per‑item overlap scores, and multi‑model replication—that will make future contamination audits sensitive to web‑sourced leakage. All execution artifacts, validator traces, reconciliation outputs, and manifests are archived in the execution bundle referenced below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
